stage_description: The juvenile stage runs from the fry period up to about 20% of the species' expected lifespan, whether that is a couple of months for a guppy or a few years for a goldfish or koi. Juveniles are still growing rapidly and beginning to show adult color and shape, with hearty appetites. Clean, stable, fully cycled water remains far more important to their health than any other single factor.
nutrition: Feed a varied, high-quality diet suited to the species — flakes, pellets, frozen or live foods, and plant matter for herbivorous fish — two or three times a day in amounts finished within a couple of minutes. Never overfeed, since leftover food breaks down and pollutes the water.
activity: Provide a tank sized for the fish's eventual adult dimensions, with plants, hiding places, and open room to swim. Choose compatible tankmates and avoid overstocking, which stresses fish and overloads the filter — a common trigger for disease.
veterinary_check_frequency: Test the water regularly for ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, and pH, and keep up routine partial water changes along with filter and temperature maintenance. Quarantine any new arrivals, and consult a vet who treats fish if signs of disease appear.
warning_signs: Clamped fins, gasping at the surface, white spots, faded color, loss of appetite, lethargy, or rubbing against objects are all warning signs. Because most illness stems from poor water quality, testing the water is the first step whenever something looks wrong.
